opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to organize the landscape is around how a model handles its state, meaning how it stores and compresses the past as it processes a sequence.

At one end you have the Transformer. Its attention mechanism effectively keeps a cache of every token it has seen, the KV cache, and at each step it can look back over all of it. That gives you an uncompressed state that grows linearly with sequence length. It's extremely powerful for precise recall, since you can retrieve exactly what you saw earlier, but it costs you: quadratic compute in training and memory that keeps growing at inference time.

At the other end are recurrent models, and this is where state space models like S4 and Mamba, linear attention variants, RWKV, xLSTM, and the newer gated linear RNNs mostly sit. They maintain a fixed-size state. Every new token has to be folded into that compressed representation, so you get constant memory and linear-time processing, which is great for long contexts and fast generation. The tradeoff is that you're forced to decide what to keep and what to throw away.

So for me, the central axis is really the degree and nature of compression. How big is the state, and how does the model decide what goes into it? A lot of the progress in this space, including the selectivity mechanism in Mamba, has been about making that compression smarter and input-dependent, so the model can choose what to remember based on content rather than applying a fixed linear filter.

Once you look at things this way, a lot of models that seem different on the surface turn out to be closely related. With Mamba-2 and the structured state space duality work, we showed that certain SSMs and certain forms of linear attention are essentially two views of the same underlying computation. Many of the recent architectures, like DeltaNet, gated linear attention, and others, can be understood as different choices about the state update rule. They differ in how they write to memory, how they decay or erase old information, and whether that update is more like a simple accumulation or something closer to an online learning step.

The practical upshot is that I don't think it's a story of one approach winning. Compressed state and uncompressed cache have genuinely complementary strengths. That's why hybrid models, which mix mostly SSM or recurrent layers with a few attention layers, work so well empirically. You get efficiency and good long-range summarization from the recurrent parts, and precise retrieval from the attention parts. The interesting research questions now are about finding the right balance along that axis, and whether we can design state mechanisms that close the remaining gap without needing the full cache.

r001.rationale: The response makes state compression the central axis and explains its efficiency and recall trade-offs, including growing inference-time memory for attention and constant memory for recurrent models.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the landscape is organized by how models handle state—how they store and compress the past—and describes that as governing the trade-off.

r003.rationale: It contrasts attention’s cache of every token with recurrent models’ fixed-size state.

r004.rationale: It identifies state update rules as a major difference, describing how models write to memory, erase or decay information, or accumulate it as new tokens arrive.

r005.rationale: It mentions simple accumulation as one kind of update, but does not say models with simple linear state updates are competitive with other post-Transformer models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the central axis is really how a model chooses to compress the context. Every sequence model has to decide what to carry forward from the past, and the two extremes are pretty clear. On one end you have attention, which doesn't compress at all. It keeps the entire history around as a KV cache and looks back over it every step, so it's lossless, but the cost grows with the sequence length. On the other end you have recurrent models, including the state space models I've worked on, where the entire history gets squeezed into a fixed-size state. That's very efficient, constant memory and constant time per token, but you're forced to be lossy, so the whole game becomes how well you decide what to keep.

So I'd frame most of the post-Transformer landscape as different points on that spectrum, plus different mechanisms for making the compression smart. Linear attention, RWKV, RetNet, Mamba, the various gated linear recurrences, they all share the fixed-state structure, and what differentiates them is the update rule. How is the state written to, how is it decayed, how much of that is input-dependent? Selectivity, which was the key idea in Mamba, was really about making that compression data-dependent so the model can decide, token by token, what's worth remembering and what to forget. And then you see hybrids that pull in a few attention layers to get back some of the lossless recall where it matters.

There's a second axis I'd add, which is more about the type of structure the state has, whether it's a vector, a matrix, something being updated by an outer product or a more expressive delta rule. But honestly that's downstream of the same question. It's all about the tradeoff between how much you store, how you store it, and how efficiently you can compute over it. I think once you see it that way, the models stop looking like a zoo of unrelated architectures and start looking like a fairly coherent design space.

r001.rationale: The response describes the trade-off between growing inference cost for attention and efficient but lossy fixed-state recurrence, linking compression quality to what the model can remember.

r002.rationale: It says the central issue is what models carry forward from the past and how well they decide what to keep, directly tying retained information to the trade-off.

r003.rationale: It contrasts attention's KV cache of the history with recurrent models that compress the history into a fixed-size state.

r004.rationale: It names recurrent models’ update rule as a differentiator and discusses writing and decaying state, but does not clearly state that the current state and next input combine to produce the next state.

r005.rationale: It lists linear attention and other architectures as sharing a fixed-state structure, but does not say that simple linear state updates are competitive with other post-Transformer models.

astra-6.text:
I think the central axis is how you represent and update the model’s state—the information it carries forward from the sequence. In a Transformer, that’s essentially the KV cache, which grows as you see more tokens. That gives you direct access to the history, but the cost grows with the sequence length.

In a recurrent model, including a state space model, you’re compressing that history into a fixed-size state. So the question becomes: what do you keep, what do you forget, and how do you make that decision depend on the input? A lot of the differences between these architectures come down to that choice of memory representation and update rule. And that choice affects both what the model can express and how efficiently you can train it and run inference.

r001.rationale: It frames state representation and updating as the central axis, then connects that choice to model capability and efficiency, including the growing inference cost of the Transformer KV cache.

r002.rationale: It says recurrent models compress history into a fixed-size state and that what they keep or forget affects both what they can express and efficiency.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Transformers’ growing KV cache with recurrent models’ fixed-size state.

r004.rationale: It mentions input-dependent state updates, but does not clearly identify combining the current state with the next input to produce the next state as a major axis among recurrent models.

r005.rationale: It does not state that models with simple linear state updates are competitive with other post-Transformer sequence models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central axis is how you represent and manage state. When you process a sequence, what information from the past do you retain, and how do you access it when the next token arrives?

With a Transformer, you essentially keep a growing record of the past in the key-value cache, and attention lets you look back over that record. With a recurrent model, including a state space model, you compress that history into a fixed-size state that you update at every step. That gives you a different tradeoff: processing can be very efficient, but the model has to decide what information to preserve.

So I tend to view these architectures in terms of their memory: how large it is, how it gets updated, and how expressive the read and write operations are. That’s often more illuminating than the particular architecture name.

r001.rationale: It mentions efficient processing and information preservation, but does not identify a performance–efficiency trade-off, particularly at inference time, as the central axis.

r002.rationale: It centers the trade-off on what past information the model retains, describing history compression as a fixed-size state and noting the need to decide what to preserve.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a Transformer's growing key-value cache, which attention reads, with recurrent models' fixed-size state.

r004.rationale: It says recurrent state is updated at every step but does not describe combining the current state with the next input to produce the next state as a major axis of variation.

r005.rationale: It makes no claim about simple linear state updates being competitive with other post-Transformer models.
